messages.content:
You are the writer of the discussion described below. You write out the discussion that the participants listed below take part in, under the rules and the flow given.

## Setting
Allocating the bicycle parking spaces. A small apartment building has fewer bicycle spaces than residents who want them, and the five members of the residents' association must decide how they are allocated. Participants: Shunichi, Toshio, Ryuji, Yumi and Asuka. Each participant has a concern of their own, which the others do not know.
Things that can be looked into (titles only):
- The building account's two-year ledger
- The ward cycle park by the station
- Treasurer's handover file on cash collections
- Trial of the supplier's display frame
- Morning departures watched from the entrance
- Rain exposure along the parking rows
- Five years of association minutes
- Sticker register and the daily riders
- Account from the neighbouring block's secretary
- Last year's complaint log entries

## Discussion format
The talk proceeds in rounds. Each round has 4 turns; in each turn, every participant speaks once, in this fixed order: Asuka, Yumi, Ryuji, Shunichi and Toshio. On a turn, a participant either speaks, says "Skip" (passes this turn only), or says "Over" (takes no further turns this round). A participant can address another directly with @Name, to ask them a question, answer theirs, agree with them, or object to what they said. An utterance is anywhere from 1 to 40 words; give it the length and content that suit the moment. An utterance consists only of the participant's own words: no name labels, headings, stage directions or commentary, and no speaking for others. The talk is a conversation among the participants: they respond to one another, asking, answering, agreeing and objecting, and the decision grows out of that exchange.

## Schedule
| Round | Start of the round | Talk | End of the round |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | nothing new (the things that can be looked into are listed above, titles only) | 4 turns | each participant chooses 2 of the listed things to look into |
| 2 | each participant is told what they found out (that participant only) | 4 turns | nothing |
| 3 | everyone is told the options | 4 turns | every participant votes; the option with the most votes is adopted |
- Several participants may choose the same thing; what is found out is told only to the participant who looked into it.
If votes are tied, one of the tied options is chosen by a fixed rule. The discussion ends after the vote.

## Looking into things
After round 1, each participant chooses 2 of the listed things to look into. What they find out is told only to that participant.

## Participants
Name: Shunichi
Age: 32
Gender: male
Personality: Shunichi is a very confident person who can remain calm in any situation. He is not modest, and has a slightly sarcastic side, but that is part of his charm. He is not sociable, but he is good at communicating at the right time and is relied upon by those around him. He rarely becomes overly emotional and can analyze situations calmly and act accordingly, so he has an unexpectedly rational side.
Concern: Every proposal that comes up at our meetings ends with someone asking what it will cost the building, and nobody has ever gone and looked. I also have no idea what a household actually pays when it ends up with nowhere to keep a bike.

Name: Toshio
Age: 28
Gender: male
Personality: Toshio has a calm and calculating personality and does not often show his emotions. He has a strong will and is the type of person who steadily moves toward his goals. He tends to take a step back from those around him, is not very assertive, and has an air of mystery about him. Occasionally, he observes things with a sharp gaze and has the ability to quickly assess situations. As a result, he is trusted by others as a reliable presence, but he is cautious about getting deeply involved with others. It seems that he has experienced some pain or suffering in his past, but he rarely shows it to others, and those scars may be connected to his cold-hearted side.
Concern: Whatever we settle on, somebody has to keep it running month after month, and the last two jobs we invented landed on one person and then quietly lapsed. I wanted to know what handling it would actually take, in paperwork and in physical effort.

Name: Ryuji
Age: 28
Gender: male
Personality: Ryuji has a calm and cautious personality, and is the type of person who always assesses the situation before acting. He rarely shows his emotions, and spends his time thinking deeply about many things. His friends consider him to be serious and reliable, but his expressionless attitude can sometimes make them feel uneasy. He tends to judge things based on reason rather than intuition, and strongly sticks to his beliefs. He is very independent and often does things at his own pace.
Concern: Getting a bike out in the morning has turned into a shoving match down there, and where yours happens to end up standing seems to decide what state it is in by the evening. Neither of those is anyone's fault exactly, which is why I went and looked properly.

Name: Yumi
Age: 16
Gender: female
Personality: Yumi has a cheerful and energetic personality. She is modest, yet she also has a kind side that cares about those around her. She has a calm personality, but she is very passionate toward her friends and family, and she cannot ignore people in trouble. She smiles at the slightest thing and spreads positive energy to those around her. She is friendly and can quickly get along with people she meets for the first time.
Concern: People have started grumbling that the same places always seem to go to the same doors, and I cannot tell whether that is how it actually happened or just resentment. Nor can I say whether the places we have now sit anywhere near where the bikes actually are.

Name: Asuka
Age: 29
Gender: female
Personality: Asuka has a calm and logical personality, rarely showing her emotions and carefully judging situations. She may seem a little unfriendly at times, but she is very thoughtful and sensitive to her surroundings. She has strong opinions and will assert herself when necessary. She is not very good at socializing, but she is serious about her work and studies.
Concern: The last thing I want is a rule that turns people who currently nod at each other in the lobby into people who time their exits to avoid it. Things down in the bike area have gone sour once or twice already, and I wanted to know what happens to a building when an arrangement like this starts to bite.

## Hidden information
The options and the full text of every card are listed here. The participants do not know them before the schedule above says so, and nothing from them may appear in the talk before the round in which it is revealed.

Options (see the schedule above):
- A: Paid Allocation. Spaces are attached to a monthly charge and held by whoever takes them up, with the income going to the building's shared account.
- B: Annual Lottery. All spaces are drawn by lot once a year among the households that apply, with the result standing until the next draw regardless of circumstances.
- C: Shared Racks. The fixed allocation is dropped in favour of open double-tier racks that anyone may use on arrival, with no space belonging to a particular household.

Cards (see the schedule above; title: text):
- The building account's two-year ledger: The shared account's ledger for the past two years covers cleaning and lighting and little else, and any capital work would need a levy on households.
- The ward cycle park by the station: The ward cycle park by the station charges 2,600 yen a month, and the notice on its gate listed fourteen households waiting for a place.
- Treasurer's handover file on cash collections: The outgoing treasurer's handover file logs about three hours a month reconciling the small cash collections already run flat by flat, and per-place billing would sit on top of that.
- Trial of the supplier's display frame: On the supplier's display frame, hoisting a loaded bike onto the upper rail took both hands and twenty seconds, and the lift spring needs greasing twice a year.
- Morning departures watched from the entrance: Over two weekday mornings watched from the entrance, eleven bikes left between seven and nine, and on four of those someone had to shift another machine first.
- Rain exposure along the parking rows: The row under the eaves stays dry, but the places past the downpipe take rain across them, and a saddle left there in winter is still wet the next morning.
- Five years of association minutes: Five years of association minutes show the covered places held by the same flats throughout, with no review of the arrangement recorded at any general meeting.
- Sticker register and the daily riders: The building's bicycle sticker register runs from no bikes to three per flat, and the households riding daily, when asked, said they would sooner pay something than be counted as one equal claim.
- Account from the neighbouring block's secretary: At the block behind the building, a monthly charge on places left three households in arrears, and their association secretary said two of them stopped coming to meetings altogether.
- Last year's complaint log entries: The building's complaint log has nine notes from last year about machines leaning on each other, and every one of them died out because there was no one in particular to ask.

## Plan
The discussion follows this plan.
- Round 1: The participants discuss the current chaos and the need for a fair system. They agree to investigate financial records, physical space usage, and historical precedents to inform their decision.
- Round 2: Participants share their findings regarding the financial state of the building, the physical difficulty of certain equipment, and the social friction caused by previous arrangements. They weigh the trade-off between administrative effort and fairness.
- Round 3: The group evaluates the three options based on the gathered evidence. They debate the merits of financial gain versus administrative ease and social harmony before voting.

Each participant's part:
- Shunichi: He focuses on the financial implications and the lack of a formal system. He argues from a perspective of fiscal rationality.
- Toshio: He is concerned with the long-term administrative burden. He evaluates options based on the effort required to maintain them.
- Ryuji: He prioritizes the physical reality of the parking area and the daily friction. He argues based on observed usage patterns.
- Yumi: She cares about fairness and the feelings of the residents. She looks for a balance between equity and community harmony.
- Asuka: She focuses on the social dynamics and the risk of creating interpersonal conflict. She argues for the most logically stable social outcome.

Write the complete transcript of the discussion in the exact Markdown format specified. Output only the transcript.

## Output format
Markdown, exactly this structure; nothing before or after it:

# shared_living_0027
## Round 1
### Talk
#### Turn 1 of 4
- **<Name>**: <utterance, or exactly Skip, or exactly Over>
(one line per participant, in the fixed speaking order; repeat for Turn 2, 3 and 4; a participant who said Over has no line in the later turns of that round)
### Action
- investigate: <Name> -> <card title>; <card title>
(one line per participant; titles exactly as listed)
## Round 2
### Talk
(4 turns as above)
## Round 3
### Talk
(4 turns as above)
### Vote
- <voter name> -> <option label>
(one line per participant)
- adopted: <label of the option with the most votes>
## Result
- adopted: <label>

# shared_living_0027
## Round 1
### Talk
#### Turn 1 of 4
- **Asuka**: We need a logical system for these spaces. The current ambiguity is just a breeding ground for future resentment.
- **Yumi**: I agree! Some people seem unhappy with how things are. We should find a way that feels fair to everyone.
- **Ryuji**: It is not just about fairness, but the physical reality. The morning rush is becoming a problem.
- **Shunichi**: Precisely. We've been drifting along without a formal rule or a budget. It's time for some actual data.
- **Toshio**: Whatever we decide must be sustainable. I am concerned about who will actually manage the system long-term.
#### Turn 2 of 4
- **Asuka**: @Toshio, that is a valid point. We should look into how other buildings handle this and our own history.
- **Yumi**: Maybe we can see if the people who use their bikes every day have a different opinion?
- **Ryuji**: I want to know exactly how the bikes are being moved and where the congestion happens.
- **Shunichi**: And I want to know the financial side. What is the cost of alternatives, and what is our current balance?
- **Toshio**: I will look into the administrative workload. We cannot afford a system that collapses in two months.
#### Turn 3 of 4
- **Asuka**: I'll check the complaint logs and the neighboring block's experience to see where things go wrong.
- **Yumi**: I'll look at the sticker register and the association minutes to see if there's a pattern of favoritism.
- **Ryuji**: I will observe the morning departures and check the rain exposure in the parking rows.
- **Shunichi**: I'll examine the building ledger and the ward cycle park's pricing for comparison.
- **Toshio**: I'll check the treasurer's handover file and the supplier's display frame trial.
#### Turn 4 of 4
- **Asuka**: Over.
- **Yumi**: Over.
- **Ryuji**: Over.
- **Shunichi**: Over.
- **Toshio**: Over.
### Action
- investigate: Asuka -> Last year's complaint log entries; Account from the neighbouring block's secretary
- investigate: Yumi -> Sticker register and the daily riders; Five years of association minutes
- investigate: Ryuji -> Morning departures watched from the entrance; Rain exposure along the parking rows
- investigate: Shunichi -> The building account's two-year ledger; The ward cycle park by the station
- investigate: Toshio -> Treasurer's handover file on cash collections; Trial of the supplier's display frame

## Round 2
### Talk
#### Turn 1 of 4
- **Asuka**: The neighboring block had residents stop attending meetings due to payment disputes. We must avoid creating financial enemies.
- **Yumi**: I found that the same flats have held the covered spots for years without any review. That explains the grumbling.
- **Ryuji**: It's worse than we thought. People are shifting other bikes just to leave, and some spots are completely exposed to rain.
- **Shunichi**: Our ledger is nearly empty; any upgrades require a levy. Meanwhile, the ward park is expensive and has a long waitlist.
- **Toshio**: The current cash collection is already a burden. Adding per-space billing would increase the treasurer's workload significantly.
#### Turn 2 of 4
- **Asuka**: @Yumi, if the arrangement has been static for five years, a sudden change might be jarring. We need a smooth transition.
- **Yumi**: But the daily riders told me they'd actually prefer to pay for a guaranteed spot than have an equal claim.
- **Ryuji**: If we keep fixed spots, the "rainy" spots will always be the source of conflict. The physical layout is the problem.
- **Shunichi**: If residents are willing to pay, we could solve our budget issues. It's the most rational way to allocate scarce resources.
- **Toshio**: @Shunichi, but who manages the money? The handover file shows the current process is already tedious.
#### Turn 3 of 4
- **Asuka**: @Toshio, is the physical effort of a new rack system any better?
- **Yumi**: I just want everyone to feel it's fair. A lottery might be the kindest way?
- **Ryuji**: A lottery doesn't fix the "shoving match" in the morning or the rain. We need a structural change.
- **Shunichi**: A lottery is a gamble. Paid allocation ensures those who value the space most get it, and the building profits.
- **Toshio**: The display frame trial showed that double-tier racks are physically demanding and require regular maintenance.
#### Turn 4 of 4
- **Asuka**: So we have a choice between administrative burden, social friction, or physical difficulty.
- **Yumi**: I'm worried that paying for spots might make some neighbors feel excluded.
- **Ryuji**: I'm more worried about the bikes leaning on each other and the morning chaos.
- **Shunichi**: Let's be realistic. We can't afford new equipment without a levy, and we can't ignore the revenue potential.
- **Toshio**: I prefer the option with the least amount of monthly paperwork and maintenance.

## Round 3
### Talk
#### Turn 1 of 4
- **Asuka**: Option A creates financial tension, B is a temporary fix, and C creates physical chaos. I lean toward B for stability.
- **Yumi**: I like B too. A lottery is fair and doesn't make people feel like they are "buying" a right.
- **Ryuji**: I strongly oppose B. It doesn't solve the congestion. Option C, shared racks, removes the "my spot" mentality entirely.
- **Shunichi**: Option C is a nightmare to maintain and expensive to install. Option A is the only one that makes financial sense.
- **Toshio**: Option C requires greasing and physical effort. Option A is a paperwork nightmare. Option B is the lowest maintenance.
#### Turn 2 of 4
- **Asuka**: @Ryuji, wouldn't shared racks just lead to more "leaning" and complaints since no one is responsible for a spot?
- **Yumi**: Exactly! And if the racks are hard to use, people will just park wherever they want.
- **Ryuji**: At least it's honest. Right now, the "covered" spots are a hidden privilege.
- **Shunichi**: @Toshio, surely the benefit of a building fund outweighs a few hours of bookkeeping?
- **Toshio**: Not if the treasurer quits. We've seen roles lapse before. I cannot support Option A.
#### Turn 3 of 4
- **Asuka**: If we go with B, we reset the unfairness Yumi found without the risks of A or C.
- **Yumi**: I agree. It's a fresh start for everyone every year.
- **Ryuji**: It's a lazy solution. We are ignoring the physical congestion and the rain.
- **Shunichi**: It's not lazy, it's just inefficient. We are leaving money on the table and ignoring the market value of the spaces.
- **Toshio**: Efficiency is useless if the system is unsustainable. B is the only one that doesn't create a new job.
#### Turn 4 of 4
- **Asuka**: It seems B is the most logical compromise for social harmony.
- **Yumi**: I'm voting for B!
- **Ryuji**: I'll stick with C, but it seems I'm outnumbered.
- **Shunichi**: I'll vote A. I cannot support a system that ignores the financial reality.
- **Toshio**: My vote is for B.
### Vote
- Asuka -> B
- Yumi -> B
- Ryuji -> C
- Shunichi -> A
- Toshio -> B
- adopted: B

## Result
- adopted: B
